title: A Court Ruling, but Families Are Still Waiting for Visas
summary: For almost a year, a family has been split between two countries while it waits for one piece of paper: a visa. Dustin Hoffman, a U.S. Army veteran, started the paperwork late last year so his wife, Gloria, could live in the United States. Gloria, who is from Colombia, stayed in Argentina with their 5-year-old daughter, Chaya, and Hoffman's 12-year-old stepson, Israel. Hoffman says he misses them every day. In January, the Trump administration stopped processing immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries. Many people were already partway through the process, and some had already been approved and were only waiting for the visa itself. Gloria is from Colombia, one of the countries on the list. In August, a federal judge ordered the ban to be lifted, but the Hoffman family still has not received its visa. The State Department has continued to ask for more proof that the family can support itself without public help. Lawyers for migrants say the family shows a wider problem. They say that, in practice, the court order has not ended the wait, because interviews and visa stamps are still moving slowly. The State Department declined to comment, saying the matter is in pending litigation, while its website says the ban is no longer in effect. The ban affected more than 280,000 people who had applied by January, according to the report. A Cato Institute analysis said it targeted thousands of close family members of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, and called it one of the most extreme legal immigration policies in U.S. history. Another applicant, Colombian researcher Dr. Fernando Lizcano, who was found qualified for an extraordinary-ability visa, is also still in Colombia waiting for final approval.
why_it_matters: This matters because a visa decision can decide whether a family lives together or apart, and a court ruling does not always end a long wait on its own.

background_read: A visa is an official paper that lets a person enter and live in another country, and an immigrant visa is for someone who plans to move there for good.
Families usually apply, show papers, and wait for an interview and a final stamp before they can travel.
A court can order a government rule to stop, but offices must still carry out each step, so waiting can go on even after a ruling.
Governments also ask applicants to show they can support themselves, so officials may ask for more proof before they finish a case.
